clinicalPearls: Acquired ectatic submucosal and mucosal blood vessels that are a common cause of obscure gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in older people
Most often found in the right colon and caecum, but they occur throughout the gut
Bleeding is typically intermittent, painless and can be occult (iron-deficiency anaemia) or overt
Associations include chronic kidney disease, aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and von Willebrand disease
Endoscopy shows characteristic fern-like or spider-like vascular lesions and allows treatment
Endoscopic ablation is first-line; refractory or diffuse cases may need medical therapy or, rarely, surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Angiodysplasia consists of dilated, thin-walled, tortuous vessels in the gut wall, thought to arise from chronic, intermittent low-grade obstruction of submucosal veins leading to dilatation of the venules and overlying capillaries and loss of precapillary sphincter competence. The fragile ectatic vessels bleed intermittently. Systemic factors that impair haemostasis, such as acquired von Willebrand syndrome in aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and platelet dysfunction in chronic kidney disease, increase bleeding from these lesions.
additionalInvestigations: Capsule endoscopy or device-assisted enteroscopy for small-bowel lesions
CT or catheter angiography during active bleeding
Full blood count and iron studies
Assessment for aortic stenosis and von Willebrand disease in recurrent cases
redFlags: Features suggesting malignancy as an alternative source
reference.prognosis: Many lesions are managed successfully with endoscopic therapy, but recurrence is common, particularly with diffuse lesions or predisposing systemic conditions.
pitfalls: Overlooking Heyde syndrome and the role of aortic valve intervention
Attributing anaemia to angiodysplasia without excluding malignancy
Missing small-bowel lesions requiring capsule or enteroscopy
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
